Szydlowiec New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Szydłowiec, Poland

Not demolished. Szydłowiec's Jewish community grew through the 18th century, and by 1921 its 5,501 Jews made up 76% of the town's population - among the highest Jewish shares of any Polish town - before most were murdered at Treblinka in 1942. This 'new' cemetery was established around 1811 beside an older cemetery already in use since the 18th century; the two plots, plus a separate 1831 cholera-epidemic section, together stretched roughly 600 metres and were progressively fenced through the 19th century. During the war it was used for executions and mass burials of Holocaust victims, and postwar individual burials continued for a time. A Holocaust memorial was erected in 1967. Unlike many nearby cemeteries, it survived largely intact: over 2,000 tombstones remain, including a rebuilt ohel of the Rabinowicz tzaddikim, making it one of the region's best-preserved Jewish cemeteries.
